This section is the book's bibliography, not argumentative prose. It runs from file page 481 to file page 489, with printed page labels 460 through 468 clearly visible at the top of each page (file page 481 shows "460 References", file page 489 shows "468 References"). Because it is a reference list, it contains no central claims, reasoning, examples, or explicit limits of the kind the task asks me to summarize. I will not invent content that is not present.

What the section does provide is indirect evidence of the book's intellectual neighborhood, which is useful for a thinking-machine design task only as a pointer, never as a demonstrated result. The entries cluster around several themes. Learnability and formal learning theory appear in Gold's "Language identification in the limit" (file page 483, printed 462) and Hamburger and Wexler's mathematical theory of learning transformational grammar (file page 485, printed 464). Constraints on generalization and the distinction between a rule's permitted scope and mere memorization are visible in titles such as Fodor and Crain, "Simplicity and generality of rules in language acquisition" (file page 482, printed 461), Gordon and Chafetz on lexical learning and generalization in passive acquisition (file page 484, printed 463), and Gropen, Pinker, and Goldberg on "constrained productivity" in locative forms (file page 485, printed 464). These titles alone do not establish what the constraints are; the arguments sit in the cited works, not here.

Representation and semantics are heavily represented: Fodor's "The Language of Thought" (file page 482, printed 461), Jackendoff's "Semantics and Cognition" and "Grammar as evidence for conceptual structure" (file page 486, printed 465), Katz and Fodor on semantic theory (file page 487, printed 466), and Keil on semantic and conceptual development (file page 487, printed 466). Compositionality and lexical structure appear in entries on causative verb formation (Comrie, file page 481, printed 460), Fodor's argument against deriving "kill" from "cause to die" (file page 482, printed 461), and Maratsos and colleagues on the productivity of the causative (file page 489, printed 468). Causation and transitivity recur in Lord's "Don't you fall me down" (file page 488, printed 467), Hopper and Thompson on transitivity (file page 486, printed 465), and Gropen and colleagues on directness of causation (file page 485, printed 464).

Analogy appears once, in Gentner's "Structure-mapping: A theoretical framework for analogy" (file page 483, printed 462). Perception, memory, time, goals, reasoning, creativity, emotions, and social cognition are not discussed in this section; only titles touching adjacent topics appear, such as Landau and Gleitman's "Language and Experience" (file page 487, printed 466) and Marin, Saffran, and Schwartz on aphasia (file page 489, printed 468). I will not force these absent topics.

Innate versus acquired capacities is signaled by Fodor's "The present status of the innateness controversy" (file page 482, printed 461), Grimshaw on the language acquisition device (file page 484, printed 463), and Grimshaw and Pinker on positive and negative evidence (file page 484, printed 463). Again, these are citations, not findings reproduced here.

Engineering implication, kept separate from any source claim: a bibliography can serve as a reading map for the design problem. The recurring concern with constrained generalization suggests that a thinking machine needs explicit scope conditions on its rules, so that a learned pattern is neither over-applied nor reduced to a lookup table. The lexical-semantic entries suggest separating a stored item from a productive operation over structured arguments. None of this is demonstrated by these pages, and none of it establishes universal learning laws; the entries concern language acquisition specifically.

Uncertainty flag: several entries contain line-break artifacts and ligature corruption (for example "ﬁ rst", "Gr owth", "conﬁ gurational"), and some page ranges or volume numbers are split across lines. No visually dependent figures or diagrams appear. Printed labels are legible throughout.
